genres.name: Gabber and Thunderdome
genres.text: In the early 1990s, DJs and producers in Rotterdam made house music harder and faster: gabber, a Dutch slang word for mate. The music ran at more than 150 beats per minute with a distorted bass drum. It came with its own youth culture, with shaved heads and tracksuits on the dance floor. In 1992 ID&T organised the first Thunderdome party. Those parties grew into events with tens of thousands of visitors.
genres.listen: Poing by Rotterdam Termination Source became a hit in 1992. Listen for the bouncing little sounds over a bass drum that hits like a hammer.

genres.name: The MiniDisc
genres.text: In November 1992 Sony released the MiniDisc, a small disc in a plastic case. Like a cassette, you could record on it yourself, but digitally and without hiss, and you could move tracks around and give them a title. In Japan it was a success. In Europe and America it stayed a product for enthusiasts. After 2000 the computer and the mp3 made it more and more unnecessary.

genres.name: 2 Unlimited: No Limit
genres.text: In early 1993 No Limit by 2 Unlimited was number one in a large part of Europe. The face of the group was Dutch: rapper Ray Slijngaard and singer Anita Doth. The music came from the Belgian producers Phil Wilde and Jean-Paul De Coster. Eurodance worked like a kit of parts: a synthesizer riff, a rap, a chorus and a break. In this way dance music from the clubs became pop music for the charts.
genres.listen: Count the parts: synth riff, rap, chorus and break. In the British version the rap is cut out, except for the word techno, and that worked for the song too.

genres.name: Prince against his record company
genres.text: On 7 June 1993, his 35th birthday, Prince changed his name to a symbol with no pronunciation. He was in a dispute with Warner Bros, which owned the recordings of his music and decided how often he could release records. On his cheek he wrote the word slave. His fight was about a question that later became more and more important: who owns the recording, the artist or the label?
genres.listen: Prince released The Most Beautiful Girl in the World himself in 1994, without Warner. It became one of his biggest hits.

tracks.title: The Most Beautiful Girl in the World

genres.name: The death of Kurt Cobain
genres.text: In early April 1994 Kurt Cobain, the singer of Nirvana, took his own life at his home in Seattle. He was 27. With Nevermind, Nirvana had defined the guitar music of the 1990s: raw, angry and full of doubt about its own fame. After his death many young people in America and England looked for a new sound. In England, bands deliberately looked the other way: at their own pop history.
genres.listen: All Apologies sounds calm and acoustic on the album MTV Unplugged in New York, recorded in November 1993. It was released only after his death.

genres.name: The Cheiron Studio
genres.text: In the Cheiron Studio in Stockholm, producer Denniz PoP made hits for Ace of Base in the early 1990s. He taught young writers, among them Max Martin, how to build a pop song that sticks right away. In 1995 We've Got It Goin' On by the Backstreet Boys came out of there. After Denniz PoP died in 1998, Max Martin carried on, with hits for Britney Spears and *NSYNC.
genres.listen: Hear how the song hardly has a quiet moment: every line leads into the next piece of the chorus.

genres.name: The name mp3
genres.text: On 14 July 1995 researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute in Germany chose the file extension .mp3 for their way of making sound smaller. Engineer Karlheinz Brandenburg had worked for years on a technique that throws away what the ear barely hears. In this way a song becomes about ten times smaller than on a CD. Brandenburg tested his work again and again with the same song: Tom's Diner by Suzanne Vega.
genres.listen: Tom's Diner is almost only a voice, with no instruments. That is exactly why Brandenburg could hear right away when his technique distorted the voice.

genres.name: The Battle of Britpop
genres.text: On Monday 14 August 1995, Blur from London and Oasis from Manchester released a single on the same day: Country House and Roll With It. Newspapers and television turned it into a contest, the Battle of Britpop. On Sunday the result came in: Blur sold about 274,000 copies in the first week, Oasis about 216,000. Blur won the chart, but Oasis would go on to win the world.
genres.listen: Compare the two: Blur with horns, a singalong chorus and irony, Oasis with a wall of guitars and a vocal line that recalls John Lennon.

genres.name: Spice Girls: Wannabe
genres.text: On 8 July 1996 Wannabe was released, the first single by the Spice Girls. The group had come together after an advertisement in a trade paper looking for young female singers. Wannabe reached number one in England and in 1997 in America too. Each member got a nickname: Ginger, Scary, Baby, Sporty and Posh. With the slogan girl power, the group sold not only CDs but also dolls, soft drinks and a film of its own.
genres.listen: Each member gets her own line and her own character, so you hear the personalities before you see them.

genres.name: Oasis at Knebworth
genres.text: On 10 and 11 August 1996 Oasis played two evenings in the park of Knebworth House, north of London, for about 250,000 people in total. More than two million people had tried to buy a ticket. It was the high point of Britpop. A large part of the crowd knew the songs from (What's the Story) Morning Glory?, one of the best-selling albums in British history.
genres.listen: Wonderwall revolves around an acoustic guitar on which a few strings keep ringing open. The chords are easy, so everyone could play along.

genres.name: Daft Punk: Homework
genres.text: In January 1997 Homework was released, the first album by the French duo Daft Punk. Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo made it in their bedroom in Paris, with cheap equipment. They did not show their faces and later wore robot helmets. Their mix of house, disco and funk was called French touch, and it showed that dance music could be made in France too.
genres.listen: Around the World repeats the title more than a hundred times. Hear how the bass line, the drums and the voice keep changing a little, so it never gets boring.

genres.name: Tupac and Biggie
genres.text: In September 1996 Tupac Shakur was shot dead in Las Vegas. Half a year later, on 9 March 1997, The Notorious B.I.G. was murdered in Los Angeles. The two rappers stood as symbols of a feud between West Coast and East Coast hip-hop, stirred up by their labels and by the media. Both murders remained unsolved for a long time. Hip-hop was in the meantime becoming the best-selling music in America.
genres.listen: Compare the sunny funk of California Love with the slower, heavy rhythm of Hypnotize: West Coast against East Coast.

genres.name: Winamp
genres.text: In April 1997 Justin Frankel and Dmitry Boldyrev, two young programmers who had studied at the University of Utah, released Winamp, a program for playing mp3s on your computer. The first version was free. From 1998 you could change its look yourself with skins. Millions of people installed it. With that, the mp3 was no longer just for technicians, but for everyone with a computer.

genres.name: Radiohead: OK Computer
genres.text: On 16 June 1997 OK Computer by Radiohead from Oxford was released in England. While Britpop looked back cheerfully to the 1960s, this album was about alienation, technology and a world moving too fast. Paranoid Android lasts well over six minutes and consists of several parts. The album was praised as one of the best ever. Radiohead would later also show how a band could sell its music without a label.
genres.listen: Paranoid Android keeps changing mood: calm, then suddenly loud and distorted, then almost churchlike with a choir.

genres.name: Cool Britannia
genres.text: In May 1997 Labour under Tony Blair won the election. On 30 July 1997 the new prime minister received Noel Gallagher of Oasis at Downing Street. Newspapers spoke of Cool Britannia: England as a land of pop music, fashion and art. After that the wave quickly ran out. Blur in fact distanced itself from the English sound and scored with Song 2, short and loud, like the American rock that Britpop had set itself against.
genres.listen: Song 2 lasts only a little over two minutes. Woo-hoo, a quiet verse and a loud chorus: Blur copied the American grunge recipe almost as a joke.

genres.name: Lauryn Hill
genres.text: On 25 August 1998 The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill was released. Hill had made her name with the Fugees and now mixed hip-hop, soul and reggae, and she both rapped and sang. In February 1999 she won five Grammys, at the time a record for a woman in one evening, including the one for best album. It was the first time a hip-hop album received that prize.
genres.listen: Doo Wop (That Thing) begins with a spoken passage and sounds like soul from the 1960s, with horns and backing vocals, but Hill raps the verses.

genres.name: Cher and Auto-Tune
genres.text: In October 1998 Believe by Cher was released. The voice had a strange, robotic effect: the pitch jumps from note to note. It came from Auto-Tune, a program from 1997 that was meant to correct wrong notes unnoticed. The producers set it extremely sharp, so that you hear it clearly. Believe became a worldwide hit. Later T-Pain, Kanye West and many rappers made the Auto-Tune sound a fixed part of pop and hip-hop.
genres.listen: Listen to the line I can't break through: the voice suddenly sounds like a machine, while the rest of the song is ordinary dance-pop.

genres.name: ...Baby One More Time
genres.text: In October 1998 ...Baby One More Time by Britney Spears was released, written by Max Martin and recorded in Stockholm. The song has no long introduction: after three hard piano chords the hook is already there. It became number one worldwide. The album of the same name sold more than ten million copies in America alone. Teenagers bought more CDs in those years than ever.
genres.listen: The hook comes in the first seconds: three piano chords and Oh baby, baby. There is no intro to skip.

genres.name: Philips sells PolyGram
genres.text: In December 1998 the Canadian company Seagram bought the record company PolyGram from the Dutch Philips and merged it with Universal Music. PolyGram had record labels such as Island, Motown and Mercury and for a long time had a head office in Baarn. Universal became the largest record company in the world. In the music industry a handful of big companies remained, just at the moment when the CD was at its peak.

genres.name: Eminem
genres.text: On 23 February 1999 The Slim Shady LP by Eminem was released, a white rapper from Detroit, discovered and produced by Dr. Dre. His lyrics were funny, nasty and often shocking, with a character, Slim Shady, who said everything that was not allowed. Parents and politicians were angry, young people all over the world bought his albums. Eminem became one of the best-selling artists of the early new century.
genres.listen: In My Name Is, Eminem introduces himself in a silly, whining little voice. The music comes from a song by Labi Siffre from 1975.

genres.name: Napster
genres.text: In June 1999 student Shawn Fanning from Boston released Napster together with Sean Parker, a program with which you could search for and share mp3s. It worked from user to user: Napster only kept a list of who had which songs, and you fetched them directly from someone else's computer. Within two years tens of millions of people were sharing music for free. Every song suddenly seemed within reach.

genres.name: The peak year of the CD
genres.text: In 1999 the music industry earned more than ever, and most of the money came from the CD. People replaced their records and cassettes with CDs and so bought the same albums a second time. Anyone who wanted one hit often bought the whole album, because single releases were becoming rarer. Only in 2023 was that amount reached again, now thanks to streaming. Adjusted for the value of money today, 1999 remains the peak year.

genres.name: *NSYNC: No Strings Attached
genres.text: On 21 March 2000 No Strings Attached by the boy band *NSYNC from Orlando was released. In the first week more than 2.4 million copies were sold in America, a record that stood for fifteen years. Bye Bye Bye was written in Stockholm, by the writers of Cheiron. It was one of the last big moments of the CD boom. A few years later such sales would be almost impossible.
genres.listen: Bye Bye Bye begins with a menacing string riff and a tight, almost electronic rhythm. The chorus is made to dance to in the video.

genres.name: Metallica against Napster
genres.text: On 13 April 2000 Metallica sued Napster. The band had discovered that I Disappear, a song for the film Mission: Impossible 2, was already circulating on Napster before it had been released. Drummer Lars Ulrich became the face of the fight, and many fans held it against him: a rich rock band attacking its own audience. Rapper and producer Dr. Dre did the same shortly afterwards.
genres.listen: I Disappear is a solid rock song with a repeated guitar riff. It leaked before it appeared on the soundtrack.

genres.name: Sensation in the ArenA
genres.text: In the summer of 2000 ID&T, the company behind Thunderdome, organised the first Sensation in the Amsterdam ArenA, a football stadium full of dancing people. From 2001 everyone had to come dressed in white. Dutch DJs such as Tiësto, Armin van Buuren and Ferry Corsten played trance: fast dance music with big, floating synthesizer chords. The party was afterwards exported to dozens of countries.

genres.name: Linkin Park: Hybrid Theory
genres.text: On 24 October 2000 Hybrid Theory by Linkin Park from Los Angeles was released. The band mixed heavy guitars with rap, scratches and electronics: nu metal. Singer Chester Bennington screamed, Mike Shinoda rapped. It became the best-selling debut album of those years. For many teenagers it was their first encounter with hard guitar music, and it showed that genres were mixing more and more easily.
genres.listen: In the End keeps switching between Shinoda's rap and Bennington's sung chorus. Hear the piano melody that runs through the whole song.

genres.name: Kazaa from Amsterdam
genres.text: In March 2001 Kazaa came out, a file-sharing program made by a Swede, a Dane and programmers from Estonia, with a company in Amsterdam. Unlike Napster, Kazaa had no central list, and that made it much harder to shut down. Buma/Stemra brought a case before the Dutch court, but in 2003 the highest court ruled that the makers were not responsible for what users shared.

genres.name: Gorillaz, a band of cartoons
genres.text: In March 2001 the first album by Gorillaz was released, a band that existed only as four drawn characters. Behind it were Damon Albarn of Blur and artist Jamie Hewlett. In videos and interviews only the cartoon characters appeared. Clint Eastwood became a hit all over Europe. Gorillaz showed that a pop star does not need a real face, an idea that would return in a very different form with artificial intelligence.
genres.listen: Clint Eastwood mixes a lazy, dub-like rhythm with a melodica and the rap of Del the Funky Homosapien. Albarn sings the chorus.

genres.name: Napster offline
genres.text: In July 2001 Napster went offline. It was precisely the central list of who shared what that proved fatal for the company: it allowed the judge to hold Napster responsible. The sharing simply went on, through successors such as Kazaa, LimeWire and BitTorrent, which had no central list. CD sales began to fall and would never recover. The public had shown that it wanted music without paying for a whole album.

genres.name: The Strokes: Is This It
genres.text: In the summer of 2001 Is This It was released, the first album by The Strokes from New York. After years of heavy nu metal they sounded bare and fast, with two guitars circling each other, like the punk and new wave of New York around 1977. British magazines were enthusiastic right away. The guitar band was cool again, and within a few years dozens of new indie bands appeared.
genres.listen: In Last Nite two guitars each play a tight little figure of their own. Hear how Julian Casablancas's voice sounds as if he is singing through an old telephone.

genres.name: The iPod
genres.text: On 23 October 2001 Apple presented the iPod in Cupertino, a small white music player with a hard disk and a scroll wheel. Mp3 players already existed, but few songs fitted on them and they were awkward to use. Steve Jobs summed up the idea in one sentence: a thousand songs in your pocket. Your whole record collection fitted in your coat, like the Walkman twenty years earlier, but without cassettes.

genres.name: Seven Nation Army
genres.text: In February 2003 Seven Nation Army came out by The White Stripes from Detroit, a duo with only guitar and drums. The riff sounds like a bass, but Jack White played it on a guitar with an effects pedal that lowers the pitch by an octave. In October 2003 supporters of Club Brugge sang the riff in Milan, and after that football fans all over Europe. In this way an indie song became an anthem without words.
genres.listen: Hear the riff: seven notes, repeated again and again. There is no real bass in the band, only a guitar that sounds like a bass.

genres.name: Idols
genres.text: At the end of 2002 Idols began on RTL, the Dutch version of the British Pop Idol: a talent contest in which viewers voted by telephone. In March 2003 sixteen-year-old Jamai Loman won. His single Step Right Up spent seven weeks at number one in the Top 40. In England and America it worked the same way, with winners such as Will Young and Kelly Clarkson. Pop stars were now chosen on television, and the public voted along.
genres.listen: Step Right Up was Jamai's single after his win. Hear how the song is made to be sung along to right away.

genres.name: The iTunes Store
genres.text: On 28 April 2003 Apple opened the iTunes Store, a shop where you could legally download music for 99 cents a song. The record companies agreed because after Napster they needed a legal alternative, and because the files were given copy protection. From now on you could buy one song instead of a whole album. The single came back, but now as a file.

genres.name: Lawsuits against downloaders
genres.text: On 8 September 2003 the American record industry sued 261 ordinary people who shared music through programs such as Kazaa. Among them was a twelve-year-old girl from New York. Her mother settled for 2,000 dollars. In the years that followed, thousands of cases followed, also against students. It mainly produced bad press, and the sharing simply went on.

genres.name: Tiësto at the Olympic Games
genres.text: On 13 August 2004 the Dutch DJ Tiësto played at the opening of the Olympic Games in Athens, while the athletes walked into the stadium. An enormous television audience watched worldwide. It was the first time a DJ was given such a place. Tiësto was voted best DJ in the world for years. The Netherlands became known as the country of the big dance producers and parties.
genres.listen: Tiësto's version of Adagio for Strings turns a sad classical piece by Samuel Barber into trance, with a driving beat.

genres.name: YouTube
genres.text: On 23 April 2005 Jawed Karim put the first video on YouTube, a site he had founded with two colleagues: not even twenty seconds, about the elephants at the zoo in San Diego. Within a few years YouTube became the biggest place to watch and listen to music, for free. Music videos, which used to be shown on MTV, could now be seen anytime and anywhere.

genres.name: The first Tomorrowland
genres.text: In August 2005 the Belgian brothers Manu and Michiel Beers organised the first Tomorrowland together with ID&T, at the recreation area De Schorre in Boom. It was one day, with Armin van Buuren among others. About nine thousand people came, far fewer than hoped, and the organisers made a loss. Even so, the festival grew into one of the biggest dance festivals in the world, with visitors from more than a hundred countries and, since 2014, two weekends.

genres.name: Arctic Monkeys
genres.text: On 23 January 2006 the first album by Arctic Monkeys from Sheffield was released. In the first week more than 360,000 copies were sold in England, the fastest-selling debut album up to then. The band had become known because fans passed around recordings of concerts and demos for free and put them on the internet, on MySpace among other places. In this way the internet became not only a place to steal music, but also a place to make fans.
genres.listen: In I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor, Alex Turner sings fast and in a broad Sheffield accent, about an evening in a disco.

tracks.title: I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor

genres.name: Raid on The Pirate Bay
genres.text: On 31 May 2006 the Swedish police raided The Pirate Bay, a website where you could find music, films and games through BitTorrent. The servers were seized, but after three days the site was back online. The makers were convicted in 2009, and the site remained. The Swedish Pirate Party gained many new members after the raid. A few years later the legal solution came from the same country: Spotify.

genres.name: OK Go on treadmills
genres.text: In the summer of 2006 the American band OK Go put a video on YouTube that they had made themselves, for almost no money. Four men dance in one long take on eight treadmills. Millions of people watched and passed it on. The video won a Grammy. A band no longer needed MTV to become famous: a clever idea and a camera were enough.
genres.listen: Here It Goes Again is a cheerful guitar-pop song. The video is one take without cuts, and the band needed seventeen attempts before everything went right.

genres.name: Amy Winehouse: Back to Black
genres.text: In October 2006 Back to Black was released by Amy Winehouse from London. With producers Mark Ronson and Salaam Remi and the musicians of the Dap-Kings she made soul that sounded as if it came from the 1960s, with honest and harsh lyrics about love and addiction. The album was a worldwide success and Winehouse won five Grammys with it in 2008. Newspapers followed her problems day and night. In July 2011 she died, aged 27.
genres.listen: In Rehab you hear horns and a rhythm like Motown soul, while Winehouse sings that she does not want to go to rehab.

genres.name: The iPhone
genres.text: On 9 January 2007 Steve Jobs presented the iPhone: a telephone, an iPod and an internet device in one. A year later came the App Store, with which you could put programs on your phone yourself. With that, the phone became the place where people listen to, discover and share music. All later apps, from Spotify to TikTok, exist thanks to the smartphone.

genres.name: Hatsune Miku
genres.text: On 31 August 2007 the Japanese company Crypton released Hatsune Miku: a program with which you could make a computer sing, with a drawn girl with long turquoise pigtails as its face. Anyone could make songs with it. Fans put thousands of songs online, and Miku later gave concerts as a hologram for sold-out halls. A singer who did not exist became a star, made by her audience.

genres.name: Radiohead: pay what you want
genres.text: On 10 October 2007 Radiohead released the album In Rainbows through its own website, without a record company. Buyers could decide for themselves how much they paid, even nothing. Many people paid something anyway, and the band earned well from it. It showed that a well-known band could sell its music itself, directly to the fans. The label was no longer a given.
genres.listen: 15 Step opens the album with a rhythm in five beats, made with a drum machine, after which guitar and real drums join in.

genres.name: Record Store Day and vinyl
genres.text: On 19 April 2008 the first Record Store Day was held, a day to support record shops, with special releases on vinyl. While the CD was disappearing, the old LP came back. Fans wanted to hold something again: a sleeve, a record, a ritual. Every year more records were sold. In 2020 more money was spent on vinyl than on CDs in America for the first time since the 1980s.

genres.name: Spotify
genres.text: In October 2008 Spotify started in Stockholm, founded by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. You no longer bought songs, but paid for access to everything: free with advertising or without advertising with a subscription. Ek wanted to make something easier than illegal downloading. In 2010 Spotify came to the Netherlands. The question shifted from do you have it? to can you get to it?.

genres.name: SoundCloud
genres.text: On 17 October 2008 SoundCloud went online, set up by the Swedes Alexander Ljung and Eric Wahlforss and based in Berlin. Anyone could upload recordings there themselves, without a record label. Listeners could comment, like and share. In this way it became a place where new talent was discovered. In November 2015 Billie Eilish and her brother Finneas put Ocean Eyes on it, so that her dance teacher could use it. The song went viral.
genres.listen: Hear how small and soft Ocean Eyes sounds: a bedroom production that found an audience without a label.

genres.name: MTV without music
genres.text: On 8 February 2010 MTV removed the words Music Television from its logo. The channel, which had started in 1981 with Video Killed the Radio Star, was by then mainly broadcasting reality series. Anyone who wanted to see a video went to YouTube, where you could look up almost any video whenever you liked. Almost thirty years after its start, MTV's work had been taken over by the internet.

genres.name: Spotify in the Netherlands
genres.text: In May 2010 Spotify came to the Netherlands. The Dutch downloaded a lot illegally, but were also quick to pay for convenience. Within a few years the Netherlands was one of the countries with the highest number of paying streamers per inhabitant. Young people especially no longer listened to CDs or the radio, but to playlists. As a result the Dutch chart would change too.

genres.name: Avicii: Levels
genres.text: In October 2011 Levels was released by the Swedish DJ Avicii, Tim Bergling, then 22 years old. The song became a worldwide hit and one of the best-known songs of the EDM wave, the big dance music that now conquered America too. DJs played for tens of thousands of people at festivals and earned millions. Avicii toured for years without a break. In 2018 he died, aged 28.
genres.listen: Levels uses a gospel-like vocal fragment from Something's Got a Hold on Me by Etta James. Hear how the song builds up to the drop, where the synthesizer melody breaks loose.

genres.name: Gangnam Style: a billion views
genres.text: On 21 December 2012 the video of Gangnam Style by the South Korean rapper PSY became the first video to be watched a billion times on YouTube. Most viewers did not understand the Korean lyrics, but everyone copied the horse dance. It showed that a hit no longer had to come from America or England. The internet had no borders, and K-pop was on its way to the world.
genres.listen: Gangnam Style revolves around a fast electronic beat and a chorus you can sing along to even without Korean. The song pokes fun at the wealthy district of Gangnam in Seoul.

genres.name: YouTube counts in the chart
genres.text: In February 2013 Billboard began to count the number of times a song was viewed on YouTube in the American chart as well. Immediately Harlem Shake by the producer Baauer was at number one. Thousands of people had made videos in which first one person dances and then, after the drop, everyone goes wild. Not the record but the video made the hit, a foretaste of TikTok.
genres.listen: After a quiet start you hear con los terroristas, and then the heavy bass drops in. In the videos, that was the moment everyone started dancing.

genres.name: Daft Punk: Get Lucky
genres.text: In April 2013 Get Lucky was released by Daft Punk, with Pharrell Williams as singer and Nile Rodgers of Chic on guitar. After years of samples the duo recorded the album Random Access Memories with real musicians in expensive studios, as a tribute to the disco of the 1970s. Get Lucky became one of the best-selling songs of the year, and the album won the Grammy for best album.
genres.listen: Hear the guitar of Nile Rodgers, who plays quick, short little chords, exactly as he did with Chic in the 1970s.

tracks.artist: Daft Punk, Pharrell Williams & Nile Rodgers
tracks.title: Get Lucky

genres.name: Martin Garrix: Animals
genres.text: In June 2013 Animals was released by seventeen-year-old Martin Garrix from Amstelveen. The song became a hit all over Europe and a fixture at festivals. Garrix had made it at home, in his bedroom studio at his parents' house. In the same year the Dutch DJ Hardwell was voted best DJ in the world. With Tiësto, Armin van Buuren and Afrojack, Dutch producers shaped a large part of EDM.
genres.listen: Animals has almost no vocals. Hear the drop: a bare, hard synthesizer riff over a stomping beat.

genres.name: Avicii: Wake Me Up
genres.text: In March 2013 Avicii played a new song with a band, acoustic guitar and a singer at the Ultra Music Festival in Miami. Part of the dance audience reacted angrily. On 17 June 2013 Wake Me Up was released as a single anyway, sung by Aloe Blacc. It reached number one in the Netherlands and Great Britain, among other countries. Avicii showed that EDM, electronic dance music, could go together with folk and country.
genres.listen: Hear how the song begins as a folk song with guitar and vocals, and then turns into a synthesizer melody for the dance floor.

genres.name: Beyoncé without an announcement
genres.text: In the night of 13 December 2013 a new album by Beyoncé suddenly appeared on iTunes, without an announcement, without a single beforehand, with a video for every song. Normally an album was announced weeks in advance. In three days more than 800,000 copies were sold worldwide, faster than ever on iTunes. A big star no longer needed the old publicity machine: social media did the work.

genres.name: Streams in the Top 40
genres.text: Since February 2014 streams from services such as Spotify have counted in the Dutch Top 40. As a result the chart changed. Dutch rappers such as Lil Kleine and Ronnie Flex, and later Boef, Frenna and Josylvio, were played little on the radio. Even so they reached high places in the chart, because young people streamed them in huge numbers. Drank & Drugs by Lil Kleine and Ronnie Flex was at number one in 2015. Nederhop became the music of a generation.
genres.listen: Krantenwijk by Lil Kleine and Boef from 2017 became big mainly through streams. Hear the calm beat and how the rappers take turns telling about the time when they still had nothing.

genres.name: Taylor Swift against Spotify and Apple
genres.text: On 3 November 2014 Taylor Swift removed all her music from Spotify. She felt the free version made music worth too little. In June 2015 she wrote an open letter to Apple, which did not want to pay creators during the free trial period of Apple Music for three months. Within a day Apple gave in. An artist could now force a tech company to listen.
genres.listen: Blank Space came out in 2014, just as Swift disappeared from Spotify. She sings about the image the media had made of her.

genres.name: Alexa, play music
genres.text: On 6 November 2014 Amazon showed the Echo, a speaker you operated with your voice: Alexa, play music. You no longer had to choose an album or song, you could also ask for something cheerful or something to cook to. Music was increasingly chosen by mood instead of by artist or genre. What played was decided by the system.

genres.name: Discover Weekly
genres.text: In July 2015 Spotify started Discover Weekly: every Monday a personal playlist of thirty songs you did not know yet. An algorithm looks at what you play and skip, and at what people with a similar taste listen to. Within a few months millions of people were listening to it. The playlist took the place of the album, and a calculation rule helped choose what you heard.

genres.name: Adele: 25
genres.text: On 20 November 2015 25 was released by the British singer Adele. In the first week 3.38 million copies were sold in America, more than the record set by *NSYNC in 2000. Adele had not put the album on Spotify, so that fans had to buy it. It worked, but it was an exception. Almost nobody else could still sell that many albums in the streaming era.
genres.listen: Hello begins softly, with piano and a low voice, and breaks out in the chorus. The song is almost five minutes long, long for a hit of that time.

genres.name: Lo-fi hip-hop to study to
genres.text: On 25 February 2017 the YouTube channel ChilledCow of the Frenchman Dimitri Somoguy from Lyon began a stream that ran day and night: lo-fi hip-hop. These are calm beats that deliberately hiss and crackle a little, like an old record. On screen a drawn girl sits studying. Millions of pupils put the stream on while doing their homework. The channel is now called Lofi Girl.

genres.name: Despacito
genres.text: In January 2017 Despacito was released by the Puerto Rican singer Luis Fonsi and rapper Daddy Yankee, in Spanish. In April a remix with Justin Bieber came out, and the song spent sixteen weeks at number one in America. The video became the most watched video on YouTube. A Spanish-language song was now a worldwide hit, and reggaeton from Puerto Rico went mainstream.
genres.listen: Hear the reggaeton rhythm, the dembow, with a kick on every beat and a skipping snare. The song begins with the cuatro, a small Puerto Rican guitar, and then the acoustic guitar of Latin pop joins in.

genres.name: Streaming becomes the biggest
genres.text: In April 2018 the international music industry reported that streaming in 2017 was the biggest source of income for the first time, at 38 per cent: more than CDs and more than downloads. After fifteen years of decline the industry had been growing again since 2015. But the money was divided differently. For each stream an artist gets a fraction of a cent, and what he keeps depends on his contract. For beginners that is often almost nothing.

genres.name: Pulitzer Prize for Kendrick Lamar
genres.text: On 16 April 2018 rapper Kendrick Lamar from Compton won the Pulitzer Prize for music, for his album DAMN. It was the first time that the prize went to an artist who did not make classical music or jazz. The jury called the album a collection of songs that show the life of Black Americans in its complexity. Hip-hop was now officially art too.
genres.listen: HUMBLE. revolves around a menacing piano riff that keeps coming back and a deep 808 bass. Kendrick raps short and sharp, almost like a sermon.

genres.name: TikTok
genres.text: On 2 August 2018 the app musical.ly, in which teenagers made videos to bits of music, was merged with TikTok of the Chinese company ByteDance. On TikTok you choose a sound clip and make a video to go with it. An algorithm decides who gets to see it. Within a few years the app became the place where hits began, and record companies started looking there for new artists.

genres.name: Old Town Road
genres.text: In December 2018 the nineteen-year-old rapper Lil Nas X from Atlanta put Old Town Road online. He had no record deal. He had bought the beat online for 30 dollars from the Dutch producer YoungKio, who had sampled a banjo fragment from Nine Inch Nails. Lil Nas X rapped about a cowboy on a horse. In early 2019 thousands of people made TikTok videos to it, in which they turned into a cowboy.
genres.listen: Hear two worlds: the banjo and the horse come from country, the deep 808 bass and the rattling hi-hats from the trap of Atlanta.

genres.name: Is it country?
genres.text: In March 2019 Billboard removed Old Town Road from the country chart: it was said to have too few country elements. Many people found that strange and asked who decides which genre a Black artist belongs to. Lil Nas X made a remix with country singer Billy Ray Cyrus. It spent nineteen weeks at number one in the Billboard Hot 100, longer than any song before.
genres.listen: In the remix Billy Ray Cyrus sings a verse of his own. With that, the question of whether it is country became hard to deny.

genres.name: Billie Eilish
genres.text: On 29 March 2019 the first album by Billie Eilish was released, when she was seventeen. She recorded it with her brother Finneas in his bedroom in Los Angeles, with a laptop and little equipment. Her music was soft and dark, often whispered. In January 2020 she won the four most important Grammys in one go. A big studio was no longer needed to become a world star.
genres.listen: In bad guy the bass sounds deep and dry, with finger snaps and whispered vocals. At the end the song suddenly changes tempo and mood.

genres.name: Duncan Laurence: Arcade
genres.text: On 18 May 2019 Duncan Laurence won the Eurovision Song Contest in Tel Aviv with Arcade, the first Dutch win since 1975. Two years later something remarkable happened: through TikTok the song became popular again, now outside Europe too. It entered the American chart in 2021 and became one of the most streamed Eurovision songs ever. An old hit could get a second life through an app.
genres.listen: Arcade begins with only piano and a soft voice. Hear how the chorus grows bigger and bigger, with a choir in the background.

genres.name: Taylor Swift's masters
genres.text: On 30 June 2019 Big Machine Records was sold, the label where Taylor Swift had released her first six albums. With that, the masters, the original recordings, passed into the hands of manager Scooter Braun. Swift had tried to buy them herself, but only received an offer under strict conditions. She decided to re-record her old albums. An artist can write and sing her own songs, and still not own the recordings.

genres.name: Bandcamp Friday
genres.text: On 20 March 2020 almost all concerts had been cancelled because of covid, and with that many musicians no longer earned anything. That Friday the website Bandcamp waived its usual share of sales. Everything went to the artists and labels. That day fans bought 4.3 million dollars of music and merchandise, fifteen times as much as on an ordinary Friday. After that Bandcamp Friday became a recurring event.

genres.name: A concert in a game
genres.text: In the spring of 2020 almost all concerts had been cancelled because of covid. On 23 April rapper Travis Scott gave a concert in the computer game Fortnite. His figure, as tall as a skyscraper, walked through the game world while the players jumped along. More than twelve million people watched at the same time. Artists gave concerts in their living rooms, on Instagram and in games. A concert no longer needed a stage.

genres.name: BTS: Dynamite
genres.text: In September 2020 Dynamite by the South Korean boy band BTS was at number one in the Billboard Hot 100, the first song by a South Korean group to do so. It was their first song entirely in English. BTS had millions of fans all over the world, the ARMY, who worked together online to push up streams and sales. K-pop was now a global industry with its own training camps for young singers.
genres.listen: Dynamite sounds like disco from the 1970s, with horns and a cheerful bass line. It was made like this to cheer up the world during the covid period.

genres.name: Olivia Rodrigo: drivers license
genres.text: On 8 January 2021 drivers license was released by seventeen-year-old Olivia Rodrigo, known from a Disney series. On TikTok millions of people made videos to the song about a broken relationship. On Spotify it broke the record for the most streams in one day for a song that is not a Christmas song. She became the youngest artist to enter at number one in the American chart straight away. In the Netherlands too it was at the top.
genres.listen: Hear the quiet beginning with only piano and vocals, and the bridge in which everything suddenly becomes loud and full.

genres.name: Wellerman on TikTok
genres.text: At the end of 2020 the Scottish postman Nathan Evans put a video on TikTok in which he sang Wellerman, a sea song about nineteenth-century whaling. Thousands of users sang along in their own videos, adding bass lines and harmonies. In January 2021 he signed with a record company and on 22 January the single came out. On 19 March 2021 Wellerman was at number one in Great Britain.
genres.listen: Hear the stomping rhythm: a sea song, a shanty, used to help sailors work together in time.

genres.name: Taylor's Version
genres.text: On 9 April 2021 Taylor Swift released Fearless (Taylor's Version), a new recording of her 2008 album. She recorded the songs almost exactly as before, but now she was the owner. Many fans streamed the new versions from then on instead of the old ones. In this way the old masters lost much of their value. Record companies reacted by forbidding artists, in new contracts, from re-recording their old songs for longer.
genres.listen: Compare Love Story from 2008 with Love Story (Taylor's Version): almost the same, but her voice is more mature and the sound fuller.

genres.name: Froukje
genres.text: In 2021 the nineteen-year-old Froukje Veenstra broke through with Dutch-language pop songs about doubt, climate and wanting to belong. Ik wil dansen from 2020 became known mainly through Spotify and social media and was heard at protests for reopening nightlife. In this way a young singer scored in Dutch without the radio first making her big. After Doe Maar and Nederhop, Dutch was once again the language of a new generation.
genres.listen: Ik wil dansen is a danceable song with a melancholy lyric. Hear how cheerful synthesizers and a sad story go together.

genres.name: Bad Bunny: Un Verano Sin Ti
genres.text: On 6 May 2022 Un Verano Sin Ti was released by the Puerto Rican rapper and singer Bad Bunny, entirely in Spanish. The album mixes reggaeton, a danceable style from Puerto Rico, with other Latin American and Caribbean music. It became the most streamed album of 2022 on Spotify and the best-selling album of that year in the United States. Never before had that happened to an album that was not in English.
genres.listen: In Ojitos Lindos, hear how Bad Bunny sings with the Colombian band Bomba Estéreo: Caribbean rhythms and Latin American sounds mixed together, all in Spanish.

genres.name: Kate Bush and Stranger Things
genres.text: On 27 May 2022 the fourth season of the Netflix series Stranger Things began. In it the character Max keeps listening to Running Up That Hill by Kate Bush from 1985. Within a few days the song was streamed almost ninety times as often on Spotify. On 17 June 2022 it was at number one in Great Britain, 37 years after its first release. Streaming gives old songs a second life.
genres.listen: Hear the drum machine that carries on like a heartbeat, and the synthesizer sound that Bush made with a Fairlight in 1985.

tracks.title: Running Up That Hill (A Deal with God)

genres.name: Beyoncé: Renaissance
genres.text: On 29 July 2022 Renaissance by Beyoncé was released, an album full of house and disco that sounds like one continuous DJ mix. With it she honoured the Black and queer club culture that house came from, and her late cousin Jonny, who introduced her to that music. The single Break My Soul uses a bit of the house hit Show Me Love by Robin S. from 1993. The album won a Grammy for best dance album.
genres.listen: Hear the house beat with a bass drum on every beat, and the organ figure from Show Me Love running underneath.

genres.name: Vinyl outsells the CD
genres.text: On 9 March 2023 the American record industry body RIAA reported that in 2022 more LPs had been sold than CDs: 41 million against 33 million. That was the first time since 1987. Midnights by Taylor Swift went over the counter 575,000 times on vinyl in its first week, a record. Even so, most people listened through streaming. Buying a record became something for fans and collectors, to have something to hold.
genres.listen: Anti-Hero came out on Midnights, the album that sold the most on vinyl in America in 2022.

genres.name: The Eras Tour
genres.text: On 17 March 2023 the Eras Tour of Taylor Swift began in Glendale, Arizona, a concert of more than three hours covering all periods of her career. It became the first tour to earn more than a billion dollars. In the cities where she played, hotels and restaurants were full. Now that music itself earned little, the biggest stars earned mainly from concerts, which became more and more expensive.
genres.listen: Anti-Hero came out in 2022. Swift sings with self-mockery that she herself is the problem, over a calm, electronic rhythm.

genres.name: Fake Drake from AI
genres.text: In April 2023 Heart on My Sleeve went viral, a song that sounded like a collaboration between Drake and The Weeknd. Neither of them had sung it. An anonymous creator had imitated their voices with artificial intelligence. Universal had the song removed from the streaming services. The question was new: who owns a voice? And what should be paid to the artists whose music was used to train a computer?

genres.name: Hip-hop turns fifty
genres.text: On 11 August 2023 rappers at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx celebrated that hip-hop was fifty years old. On 11 August 1973 DJ Kool Herc played at a party given by his sister Cindy Campbell, in an apartment building on Sedgwick Avenue. He played the drum part of a record, the break, again and again, using two copies on two turntables. People began to dance and rap to that rhythm. That is how hip-hop began.
genres.listen: Hear the bongos and the drums in the break: exactly this kind of passage is what Kool Herc played again and again.

genres.name: Beyoncé: Cowboy Carter
genres.text: On 29 March 2024 Cowboy Carter by Beyoncé was released, a country album. Beyoncé comes from Houston in Texas and said she made the album because she had once felt unwelcome in the country world. She became the first Black woman with a number one on the American country albums chart. Five years after Old Town Road it was once again about the question of who gets to make country.
genres.listen: Texas Hold 'Em begins with a banjo and a fiddle, but the rhythm to dance to comes from R&B. Hear the stomping feet and handclaps.

genres.name: A thousand streams or nothing
genres.text: From April 2024 Spotify only pays for a song if it has been played at least a thousand times in a year. The service said these were very small amounts, which often did not reach the creators anyway. Critics felt that this meant beginning artists in particular earned nothing. The money went even more to those who were already popular. It shows that the rules of one company determine what music earns.

genres.name: Joost Klein: Europapa
genres.text: In March 2024 Europapa by Joost Klein from Friesland became a hit on TikTok and Spotify. It was at number one in the Netherlands and Flanders and also scored in other European countries. The cheerful, chaotic song is about travelling freely through Europe, and also about his late father. After an incident behind the scenes, Joost was removed from the contest on 11 May, the day of the final in Malmö. The song stayed popular afterwards.
genres.listen: Europapa sounds like a gabber party with a childlike chorus. Joost sings in Dutch and raps about the countries of Europe.

genres.name: A band that does not exist
genres.text: In the summer of 2025 The Velvet Sundown suddenly had more than a million listeners a month on Spotify. The band sounded like calm rock from the 1970s. After questions from journalists it turned out that the music, the photos and the stories had been made with artificial intelligence. Nobody played on it. Streaming services had to decide whether to label AI music, and listeners wondered what an artist actually is.
